newsitem.title: CHINA: China moves to boost commercial housing sales.
newsitem.headline: China moves to boost commercial housing sales.

text.p: China will trim taxes, bank interest rates and profits of developers and introduce mortgage loans to bolster the flagging commercial housing sector, Construction Minister Hou Jie said on Tuesday.
"The central government will push taxes down a little and local governments will push fees down a little," Hou told a news conference.
"Banks will push interest rates down a little and developers will push profits down a little... to boost housing sales," the minister said.

By the end of 1995, China had about 30 million square metres (320 million sq ft) of vacant residential housing in cities due to soaring prices and excessive investment, Hou said, but gave no value for the unused housing in a country where many urban residents live in cramped conditions.
China had about 23.54 million square metres (253.4 million square feet) of vacant urban commercial housing a year earlier, newspapers have said.
The new measures were designed to lift China's troubled real estate market out of a three-year slump.
Most urban Chinese complain they cannot afford to buy even the cheapest accommodation on the private market.

A two-bedroom apartment on the outskirts of Beijing can cost anywhere from 200,000 yuan ($24,000) to 400,000 yuan ($48,000) compared with an average annual income of 4,300 yuan ($518) for urban residents.
Housing is most expensive in Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou, Minister Hou said, quoting a survey by the State Statistical Bureau.
China plans to introduce in major cities before July a programme that would allow a buyer to pay a downpayment of 30 percent of the value of residential housing, officials said.
The remainder would be amortised for between five and 20 years, the officials said.
Chinese citizens with a stable income and the ability to repay mortgage loans would be eligible to apply, Hou said. He gave no further details.
The quality of housing in China was a crippling problem.
Urban houses covering an area of 30 million square metres (320 million square feet) are deemed "dangerous" to live in and need renovation, officials said.
Three million urban residents live in houses with an area of less than four square metres (43 square feet) each, they said.
To ease a dearth of affordable housing, the government plans to build an average of 240 million square metres (2.6 billion square feet) of housing each year through the year 2000, the officials said.

Housing was once an integral part of China's cradle-to-grave socialist welfare system, with virtually all urban residents living in housing allocated to them by their work units. This ended in the late 1980s when the government began an experiment with commercial housing. ($1 = 8.3 yuan)
